Exclude question restatements, recommendations and explicit uncertainty from facts; inventory uncertainties separately. Give an exact source_quote for every item. Map an actually supplied URL when present, distinguishing homepage_only, claim_specific and none. citation_links recovers the address of a citation actually printed in that response; it is not new evidence. Preserve any unresolved citation refs separately. Do not infer facts from external knowledge or from the query/document logs. Deduplicate repeated facts within a run. Return reviewed_runs, facts, uncertainties and omissions/limits. No gold or other files.

For this small, isolated library, I would start by comparing BookDB2 on Windows with Tellico on Linux. GCstar is another lightweight collection-manager option. BiblioteQ and Data Crow are worth considering if their extra configuration is acceptable.

I treated “users” as library borrowers, since you also ask for no logins. I did not install or operate these programs, so the exact no-login startup remains unverified. The sources establish useful catalogue and lending capabilities, but do not establish that every candidate meets every requirement.

## Ranked candidates

1. **BookDB2 — strongest direct Windows workflow match.** Its developer describes books with authors, categories and publishers, plus borrower records, multiple copies and loans. The FAQ describes local DAT files and copying the data folder for backup, which suits an isolated computer. The download page calls it free software. The FAQ also describes changing labels through language-template fields. This is particularly close to your requested list-and-lending workflow. Caveats: I did not establish an open-source license or test for a login prompt, and the developer says development of BookDB3 stalled and BookDB2 will not be updated. Sources: https://spacejock.com/BookDB.html ; https://spacejock.com/BookDB_Faq.html ; https://spacejock.com/BookDB_Download.html . The retrieved feature/download pages were last modified on 1 August 2026, so this run has not established the same capabilities were available by 4 February 2017.

2. **Tellico — strongest documented Linux alternative.** This GPL collection manager supports manual book entry, authors, grouping, custom fields and translations. It saves its data as XML without a database server. The official changelog also documents loan and borrower integration. That makes a desktop collection manager a plausible way to cover your needs with less administration than a full ILS. Check whether its borrower handling is sufficient and install the KDE dependencies before the machine is disconnected. Linux is the platform clearly supported by the retrieved overview; I did not verify a Windows package or an explicit no-login guarantee. Sources: https://tellico-project.org/about-tellico/ ; https://tellico-project.org/tellico-changelog/ . The changelog dates Tellico 3.0 to 8 November 2016 and 2.3.12 to 29 January 2017, establishing pre-cutoff releases, although the overview describes the current product.

3. **GCstar — a configurable catalogue with borrowing records.** Its official documentation lists books, Linux and Windows, open-source availability, custom collections and borrowed-item management. The borrowing guide shows a list of potential borrowers and an item's lending tab containing the borrower and lending date. This could cover a straightforward book list and loan register. Check its book-specific fields and startup behavior: the guide illustrates a movie collection and says the mechanism can apply to other collections. Email reminders would be unusable on the disconnected machine, while the documented borrower-record workflow is separate from sending mail. Sources: https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/ ; https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/usage/borrowing/ ; https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/news/ . Official news dates version 1.7.1 to 9 March 2016, but the main documentation was updated in 2022, so not every current feature or platform package is established for the cutoff.

4. **BiblioteQ using SQLite — a fuller local library option.** BiblioteQ is BSD-licensed library and archival software with a Qt desktop interface, members and circulation-related features. Its SQLite path is relevant to a single isolated machine, and the official release history documents SQLite on Windows and member-query fixes in 2016. It may require more setup and expose more library-management features than you want. I could not independently confirm the precise no-login behavior. Source: https://textbrowser.github.io/biblioteq/ . Releases dated 6 December and 5 November 2016 establish pre-cutoff availability; later features on the same live page were not assumed to exist then.

5. **Data Crow — flexible local cataloguing and loans.** The official site describes a free open-source collection manager with books, local storage, customizable fields/categories and loan administration. This is useful if tailoring the catalogue is valuable. It may be more configurable than your simple workflow needs. The opened official material did not settle the exact Windows/Linux package or whether the intended standalone mode avoids login. Source: https://datacrow.org/ . I did not open a dated primary release establishing its capabilities by the 2017 cutoff, so its historical status remains unknown.

For a practical selection, the decisive check is a short offline trial: open the program without creating an account, add a book and a borrower, record a loan and return, then close and reopen the catalogue. That would resolve the largest remaining fit question without requiring an extensive ILS setup. Online metadata lookups should be treated as optional because your machine has neither LAN nor WAN access.

Research limitations: the unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt was blocked. I used web-indexed public-code search as a fallback, but both the GitHub schema page and its raw representation were inaccessible; this was not a successful native code search. No target question answers were used, no runtime fit was tested, and release dates were distinguished from current documentation.

## Recommendation

**JSAP is the closest direct API match I found, but I cannot yet call any candidate a fully verified match for every requirement.** Its documented `parse(String)` method takes a complete command string and returns a `JSAPResult`. That distinguishes it from parsers that expect the shell to have already produced an argument array. [JSAP parsing API](https://www.martiansoftware.com/jsap/doc/ch04s04)

I treated the single-file design, non-copyleft license, and `java.util.Map` result as preferences because you explicitly placed them under “Ideal, but not necessary.” I did not turn those preferences into exclusions.

### 1. JSAP — the closest whole-parser candidate

Configure its switches and options, then call `parse(String)`. Its tokenizer documents quoted values containing spaces and escaping for quotes and backslashes. However, it describes Windows 2000-style tokenization; I would not assume full Unix-shell quoting semantics from that description. [Tokenizer documentation](https://www.martiansoftware.com/jsap/doc/javadoc/com/martiansoftware/jsap/CommandLineTokenizer)

The opened documentation establishes a string entry point and long/short option objects. I could not verify clustered `-abc`, the exact attached-equals case, or `--` termination from the pages successfully read. Nor did I establish a complete platform/runtime support matrix. These are unresolved checks, not evidence of non-support. The public parser-source retrievals failed. [Core API](https://martiansoftware.com/jsap/doc/javadoc/com/martiansoftware/jsap/JSAP) [Flagged options](https://www.martiansoftware.com/jsap/doc/ch07)

The v2.1 manual identifies LGPL, which misses your preferred licensing style but does not disqualify it under your stated requirements. Its result object is library-specific, so a small wrapper would be needed for a map-based interface. [License](https://www.martiansoftware.com/jsap/doc/pr01) [Result contract](https://www.martiansoftware.com/jsap/doc/ch04s04)

**Decision: retain for evaluation; insufficient evidence for unconditional adoption.** The next decisive check is a configured parse of `-abc --message="hello world" -- -x`, with expected flags a/b/c, one message value, and a literal trailing operand, together with verification of the target Java runtimes. Passing the listed requirements would support a direct recommendation; a documented failure of any mandatory behavior would exclude it as a whole solution.

### 2. JOpt Simple — a strong option-recognition component

Its API documents short-option clustering, long options with equals values, and `--` termination. It returns an `OptionSet` and takes separate argument tokens through `parse(String...)`. The same API page identifies MIT licensing. Do not mistake the string varargs signature for a complete-command-string lexer. [JOpt Simple API](https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/apidocs/joptsimple/OptionParser.html)

For your shell, the explicit integration would be: tokenize the line into `String[]`, pass those tokens to `OptionParser.parse`, and expose the results through your own return interface. JSAP's `CommandLineTokenizer.tokenize(String)` provides one documented token-array boundary, although that carries the JSAP quoting and licensing considerations above. A custom tokenizer is another implementation option, but none was implemented or verified here. This proposal applies to the option-recognition stage; it is not a claim that JOpt alone satisfies your string-function requirement. Incorrect tokenization would break quoted whitespace before JOpt sees the values.

**Decision: retain as a component, with integration and platform verification outstanding.** The opened JOpt documentation is version 6.0-alpha-3 and postdates your December 2015 question. Its behavior and license must not be silently attributed to an earlier release.

### 3. JArgs — a smaller option-recognition alternative

The project describes a compact Java parser with BSD licensing. Its API covers GNU-like short and long options, equals values, and `--`. Boolean short flags can be grouped, but grouped options requiring values have restrictions. [Project](https://jargs.sourceforge.net/) [API](https://jargs.sourceforge.net/doc/api/jargs/gnu/CmdLineParser.html)

It accepts `String[]`, and parsing itself returns void; options and remaining operands are retrieved through accessors. It would need the same tokenizer boundary plus a result wrapper. I did not verify that the complete integration fits in one source file or establish all-platform support.

**Decision: retain as a component, not a verified whole solution.** First confirm the tokenizer-to-array-to-accessor wrapper against the same command example and intended runtimes. The project page records a 2005 release and a 2009 modification date; the exact live API-page publication date is unknown.

For the prototype, I would investigate JSAP first because it directly accepts the required input shape. If its remaining mandatory checks pass, wrap its result behind your own interface so that replacing the implementation later is straightforward. If its behavior fails a mandatory check, JOpt Simple or JArgs remain useful parser components once the string-tokenization layer is concretely supplied. No library was installed or executed in this review.

## Recommendation

I would start with **GLib’s GOption parser**, followed by **argparse (the C library)** and **Argtable3**. None is a fully verified match to every requirement on the evidence I could inspect. In particular, I would keep unknown-option preservation distinct from merely accepting positional arguments, and verify repeated-value policies before committing to a library.

### 1. GLib GOption — the strongest documented starting point

GOption uses a table of option declarations and a parser call. It generates help, associates short and long names, and leaves positional arguments available to the application. Its documentation also describes Windows command-line encoding and a Unicode-aware parsing route. [Parser overview](https://docs.gtk.org/glib/goption.html)

Enable `g_option_context_set_ignore_unknown_options(context, TRUE)` to retain unknown options in `argv`. The documented caveat matters: the parser cannot reliably tell whether a separate non-option token belongs to a preceding unknown option. Design the handoff to your next parser accordingly. [Unknown-option setting](https://docs.gtk.org/glib/method.OptionContext.set_ignore_unknown_options.html)

Both `--foo=bar` and `--foo bar` are documented. String and filename array types collect repeated occurrences. I did not establish the exact encounter-order guarantee or scalar last-value-wins behavior from the implementation, so those remain checks rather than promises. [Argument types](https://docs.gtk.org/glib/enum.OptionArg.html)

GLib exposes a C API and identifies its license as LGPL-2.1-or-later. Its README offers public downloads and an explicit support policy for recent release series. This is a broader utility-library dependency, so consider that integration cost. I also did not open a definitive macOS support statement for the selected release. [Library and license](https://docs.gtk.org/glib/index.html) · [Downloads and support policy](https://github.com/GNOME/glib/blob/main/README.md)

For your preferences, the declaration-table approach avoids extensive macro-driven parsing logic and reuses definitions for help. A subcommand dispatch design was not verified here.

**Assessment: INSUFFICIENT for an unconditional all-requirements recommendation**, but first to evaluate. Confirm the target release’s three-platform coverage and repeat-value contracts; positive evidence for those gaps would make it a documented direct fit.

### 2. argparse — a smaller C alternative to investigate

The project describes a high-level C parser with automatic help and positional/optional arguments, and identifies an MIT license. Its README links a subcommand example. [Project](https://github.com/cofyc/argparse)

The public header exposes short and long names, a callback hook, and `ARGPARSE_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_ARGS`. These are useful building blocks, but a flag name alone does not prove unknown tokens survive unchanged. The inspected header also uses convenience initializer macros; your preference against heavy macros is not a mandatory prohibition. [Header](https://github.com/cofyc/argparse/blob/master/argparse.h)

Before selecting it, verify supported builds on all three systems, maintenance of the chosen version, both long-value spellings, unknown-token recovery, scalar overriding and ordered accumulation. Callback-based accumulation may require application code; I did not verify that implementation.

**Assessment: INSUFFICIENT**, retained because no decisive mandatory violation was established.

### 3. Argtable3 — a useful declarative alternative, with a pass-through question

Argtable3’s tutorial describes an ANSI C library under the 3-Clause BSD license. One argument table drives parsing and help, supports tagged and positional values, and permits multiple occurrences and multiple aliases. It includes Windows and GCC build instructions. [Tutorial](https://www.argtable.org/tutorial/)

The unresolved issue is whether the selected release can recover unknown options intact for another parser. A relevant project issue surfaced, but access failed. I also did not establish current maintenance, macOS coverage, separate-value long-option syntax, or the required overwrite and ordering policies. These gaps are not evidence of non-support. [Project](https://github.com/argtable/argtable3)

**Assessment: INSUFFICIENT** pending an applicable documented configuration.

### Evidence limits

This is a documentation-based shortlist, not a build or integration test. The GLib pages inspected identify version 2.91.0 and a 2026 documentation generator, so they postdate the question of 12 November 2024. The Argtable3 tutorial is dated 9 April 2014; the live repository revisions have unknown dates. I therefore do not claim that every observed current feature was available on the original question date. Anonymous GitHub code search was attempted and blocked; subsequent public GitHub-targeted web searches served as the code-through-web fallback.

HESK is the strongest starting point from this search, with LibreKB as a focused knowledge-base alternative and DokuWiki as a different implementation approach. None has been benchmarked or installed on your Windows server during this research, so I cannot promise better speed or fewer defects than your existing installation.

1. HESK — https://www.hesk.com/

The self-hosted download is free. Its public demonstration exposes article headings and bodies, categories, search, and downloadable attachments without asking the reader to log in. The official changelog records knowledge-base article keywords and a knowledge-base-only mode. These are unusually close to the content and access pattern you described. The documentation identifies version 3.7.13 as released on 18 October 2026, before the question date.

Useful primary sources: https://www.hesk.com/demo/knowledgebase.php?article=3 and https://www.hesk.com/help/docs/changelog.html.

The main tradeoff is that HESK is still a help-desk application containing ticket-management features. The knowledge-base-only mode is therefore particularly relevant, but its exact configuration and the staff editing workflow need a practical check. I did not verify its Windows/IIS requirements or SSO integration. The official search troubleshooting result also describes MySQL full-text limitations, so test your actual vocabulary and a small sample of articles instead of assuming that every short keyword will be found.

2. LibreKB — https://github.com/michaelstaake/LibreKB/

This free, open-source PHP/MySQL knowledge base provides article editing, nested categories, user groups, and downloadable article attachments. Its README describes a public site and an administrative login, making it a promising starting point for public reading with controlled editing. It appears more directly focused on publishing a knowledge base than a community Q&A application, although that does not establish that it has a smaller runtime footprint.

The important gap is keywords: the current README explicitly describes search over article titles and content, and I did not find a separately verified keyword field. If keywords must be hidden metadata, expect to investigate or add that capability. The current installation instructions require PHP 8.4 or newer and a server that honors .htaccess rewriting. Apache on Windows would be a plausible deployment route, but that is an inference, not a verified Windows deployment; IIS would require checking equivalent rewrite behavior. SSO was not established. The opened README was live and undated, so I cannot establish that these exact features and requirements were available by 21 October 2026.

3. DokuWiki with the Tag plugin — https://github.com/dokuwiki/dokuwiki
Tag plugin: https://github.com/dokufreaks/plugin-tag

A wiki can represent each FAQ as a titled page, with the Tag plugin providing category-style labels. The PHP installer source contains access-control configuration separating everyone from registered users, administrator creation, and file-based page and media directories. That provides concrete components for an FAQ with restricted authoring and a different storage approach.

This is an adaptation route rather than a fully verified replacement. It departs from the MySQL preference, requires configuring the access policy and organizing pages as FAQs, and may need additional work to make tags behave like the desired search keywords. The main DokuWiki documentation request failed with HTTP 402; I verified the public repository, installer code, and the Tag plugin description instead. Windows installation, the complete attachment workflow, and SSO remain unverified in this run. The source branches were live and lacked usable publication dates.

I would evaluate HESK's knowledge-base-only mode first, and compare LibreKB if a focused article interface matters more than a dedicated keyword field. DokuWiki is worth considering if you can accept the wiki model and file-based storage. For any of them, the decisive checks are anonymous search and attachment access, authenticated editing, matching your actual search terms, and installation on the specific Windows/PHP stack. These searches establish candidates and concrete gaps; they do not establish production suitability.

I would start with **Caddy using its file_server and templates handlers**. **nginx with SSI** is a credible second approach. Both have documented building blocks for serving files and assembling HTML inside the web server, so your shared site's page-fragment handling need not introduce a separate application-server process. I cannot certify either as “as secure/minimalist as possible”: those requirements depend on the configuration and on what amount of hardening you find acceptable.

### What “HTMX-aware” needs to mean here

HTMX normally consumes HTML responses, often fragments. A useful interpretation of your requirement is that a direct page visit receives a complete document, while an HTMX request can receive just the relevant content. The official documentation describes distinguishing these using HX-Request. When the same URL has those two representations, it also calls for Vary: HX-Request; history restoration and cache validators need corresponding care. Simply fetching a static fragment does not, by itself, solve composition of all shared page content and metadata. [HTMX documentation](https://htmx.org/docs/)

### 1. Caddy with templates — my first option to evaluate

Caddy's file server provides the static-file side. Its template handler can process file responses and include other HTML files. The template API exposes request headers through .Req.Header.Get, so you can use HX-Request to choose whether to include the surrounding page layout. Shared layout files can hold common content, while page-specific files supply each page's material. This is a mapping of documented capabilities, not a claim that I ran your site or found a turnkey HTMX preset. [File server](https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/file_server) · [Templates](https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/templates) · [Template API](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2/modules/caddyhttp/templates)

The same template API supports front-matter metadata and additional template functions, which is relevant to separating common and page-specific metadata. The installation documentation covers Linux distributions and Windows installation options. The examined package documentation identifies an Apache-2.0 license, and the project describes itself as free and open source. I did not verify a specific Alpine package or image. [Installation](https://caddyserver.com/docs/install) · [Template API and license](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/caddyserver/caddy/v2/modules/caddyhttp/templates)

The security qualification matters for your particular concern. Caddy documents protection against directory traversal in request paths, but explicitly warns that symlinks inside the site root can expose files outside it. Its template facility can access files, environment variables, and network resources. Use a dedicated public content tree, controlled symlinks and filesystem permissions, and only trusted template content. The presence of a configured root alone does not prove isolation. Whether that constitutes “really easy to secure” for you remains unconfirmed. [File-server boundary](https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/file_server) · [Template trust warning](https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/templates)

One temporal limitation: the source-derived API reference I read is Caddy v2.11.9, published November 4, 2026, after your July 25 question. The undated live guides do not establish historical availability. Confirm the chosen release's behavior before relying on this as a date-specific recommendation.

### 2. nginx with SSI — a second configuration to consider

nginx can serve static files and process Server Side Includes in the same server. Its SSI module supports file includes and conditional comparisons; its core exposes arbitrary request headers as variables. Consequently, the documented mechanisms map HX-Request to $http_hx_request and allow the shared wrapper to be included conditionally. No proxy or FastCGI backend is needed for local static-file includes. [SSI module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_ssi_module.html) · [Header variables](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html)

The official overview documents a modular architecture, a 2-clause BSD license, and Linux and Windows among tested platforms. SSI must be enabled, and its documented conditional nesting is limited. This option leaves you responsible for more of the layout and server configuration; I have not established that its hardening is sufficiently easy or its packaged feature set sufficiently minimal for your preferences. Alpine-specific packaging also remains unchecked. [nginx overview](https://nginx.org/en/) · [SSI configuration and limits](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_ssi_module.html)

### 3. lighttpd with mod_ssi — retain as an unverified lead

Official search results point to a mod_ssi module for file inclusion, but the documentation page returned HTTP 403 when opened. I therefore cannot verify the precise request-header/conditional-template integration, Linux configuration, or security fit within this run. This is a lead for further checking, not an established replacement. Missing access is not evidence that lighttpd cannot meet your requirements. [Official mod_ssi page](https://redmine.lighttpd.net/projects/lighttpd/wiki/Mod_ssi)

For your next concrete decision, evaluate a small Caddy configuration on the intended Linux environment with one shared layout and two page files. Confirm a full document on direct visits, the intended fragment on HTMX requests, correct caching/history behavior, and the filesystem boundary you expect. That would resolve the largest practical uncertainties without requiring a separate application server merely to assemble page pieces.

Python is a convenient choice for a short crawling script, and Java is also a viable choice. The important distinction is between the programming language and the mechanism used to obtain the data. Selenium is a browser automation component available to both languages; it is not a Python-only crawler.

### Why Python is often a reasonable recommendation

Python's own tutorial emphasizes its high-level data structures, dynamic typing and suitability for scripting and rapid development. That supports an expectation of convenient experimentation, not a measured claim that every developer will finish faster in Python. Existing familiarity can outweigh language-level convenience. The relevant Python ecosystem also has separate components for HTTP requests, HTML parsing and complete crawling workflows, described below. [Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3.11/tutorial/)

Selenium is useful for a different reason: it can operate the browser workflow that exposes the desired data. Its official Java and Python examples both navigate, locate elements, enter text, click and read the result. Its value therefore depends on whether the target needs that workflow, not on choosing Python. [Selenium examples](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/)

### Existing components worth considering

1. **Selenium WebDriver, in Python or Java.** Use it when browser interaction or rendered DOM state is necessary. This covers the browser-facing part of the collector; browser lifecycle, synchronization and extraction logic still need attention. It is not itself a complete crawl scheduler and output-processing system. [Documentation](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/)

2. **Requests plus Beautiful Soup, in Python.** Requests supplies HTTP requests and text or JSON responses; Beautiful Soup supplies HTML/XML tree navigation and field extraction. Together they are a straightforward starting point for a small collector whose data is already present in a response. Neither executes a site's JavaScript. [Requests](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/quickstart/) · [Beautiful Soup](https://www.crummy.com/software/BeautifulSoup/bs4/doc/)

3. **jsoup, in Java.** The official recipe fetches a URL and parses its HTML through a compact Java API. This gives a concrete answer to the concern that Java lacks an ordinary scraping option: it can collect server-returned HTML without Selenium. The recipe does not turn the parser into a browser. [Fetch-and-parse recipe](https://jsoup.org/cookbook/input/load-document-from-url)

4. **Scrapy, in Python.** For a multi-page crawler, its existing request scheduling, link-following, CSS/XPath extraction, concurrency controls and output facilities can reduce the amount of infrastructure to build. It introduces a framework to learn, and browser-specific interaction still needs another mechanism or integration. [Scrapy 2.8 overview](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.8/intro/overview.html)

### What disadvantage does Java introduce?

There is no demonstrated general loss of browser capability from using Java with Selenium. The displayed Java example has more class/method scaffolding and build configuration than the Python example, so a small exploratory script may involve more ceremony. That is an observation about these examples, not a universal productivity ranking. [Selenium examples](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/)

If a chosen tutorial or processing pipeline depends on Python packages, using Java means selecting Java equivalents or adding an integration boundary; that is a conditional engineering cost. Conversely, if the developer already knows Java or the collector belongs in an existing Java application, reuse of that knowledge and environment can favor Java. These are decision considerations, not benchmark results. The supplied question does not establish which applies.

### A practical selection sequence

First inspect a representative page and determine where its data comes from. Scrapy's versioned guidance recommends locating the underlying response and reproducing the relevant HTTP request when practical, including cases where the visible page loads data dynamically. A JavaScript-heavy interface does not by itself prove that every item must be collected through a browser. Use browser automation when the required state or interaction makes that the appropriate route. [Dynamic-content guidance](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.8/topics/dynamic-content.html)

Then choose the language according to existing skill, integration requirements and the components actually needed. A Java developer could reasonably start with jsoup for returned HTML and Java Selenium for browser workflows. Someone comfortable with Python could start with Requests and Beautiful Soup, use Selenium when necessary, and consider Scrapy as crawl orchestration grows. No target site, volume or prior skill was provided, so the evidence does not justify declaring one language universally faster, easier or more reliable.

Historical evidence is mixed. Scrapy 2.8.0 is explicitly dated 2023-02-02 in its [release notes](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.8/news.html), and the jsoup recipe is dated 2010-02-01. The other opened pages are live documentation or live code; their exact contents were not verified as available by the question date, 2023-04-12. An unauthenticated grep.app search failed; the fallback inspected public Selenium code through web search, rather than claiming native code-search success.

# Choosing between a tiny function and a library

The useful distinction is the amount of behavior and risk you would take responsibility for, rather than the number of functions you call. For a small, stable helper whose behavior you can fully specify and test, owning a local implementation can be reasonable. For cryptography, a short API call hides requirements concerning algorithms, randomness, nonces, authentication, and implementation behavior; replacing the library can transfer much more work than its call-site size suggests.

I would compare the two choices using a short ownership-cost worksheet: initial implementation or integration, review and tests, transitive dependencies, expected updates, failure consequences, and the effort needed to replace the component. This worksheet is my synthesis of the sources below, not an established quantitative scoring standard. The question does not specify a language, platform, or cryptographic operation, so the concrete libraries are examples to assess against those requirements.

## Ranked candidates

1. **GitLab's dependency evaluation process** — https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/security/best-practices/supply-chain-security-for-dependencies/

   This is the closest ready-made checklist for the decision itself: compare the amount of functionality needed, the feasibility and maintenance cost of local code, problem complexity, and transitive dependencies. It then adds project-health and security-review considerations. Adapt those questions into a brief decision record for each proposed dependency. The live page has no verified publication date in this run, so its availability on 20 April 2018 is unknown.

2. **libsodium's higher-level cryptographic APIs** — https://doc.libsodium.org/doc/quickstart

   This is a concrete example of choosing a library because the implementation obligations exceed the apparent size of the requested function. The quickstart recommends higher-level APIs and distinguishes authenticated encryption from a raw stream cipher. Use it to narrow the task to a supported operation and assess integration effort. It still requires correct key handling, initialization, and operation-specific usage; adopting a library does not finish the surrounding security design. The inspected documentation is live, and its exact pre-cutoff contents were not established.

3. **The Go Proverbs small-copying principle** — https://go-proverbs.github.io/

   This provides a useful counterweight to automatic dependency adoption: for a genuinely small, comprehensible helper, consider taking ownership of a local copy or implementation. My application of the principle is to require a clear specification, appropriate licensing for copied code, tests, and an identified maintenance owner. It does not justify rewriting security-sensitive algorithms merely because the desired interface is small. The page attributes the proverbs to a 2015 talk, but the live list can change and I did not inspect a dated recording; historical availability of this exact page is therefore left unknown.

4. **TweetNaCl.js** — https://github.com/dchest/tweetnacl-js

   This offers another point on the spectrum: a focused cryptographic implementation with a thin JavaScript API, instead of implementing primitives yourself or assuming that every library must be a broad framework. Its repository documents both a close translation and an optimized variant. A primary [Cure53 report](https://cure53.de/tweetnacl.pdf), dated 13 February 2017, establishes a pre-cutoff audit of the project. That assessment is limited to its reviewed scope and time; it is not proof that every version or protocol is secure. The current README warns that complete protocols and JavaScript side-channel constraints remain application concerns.

5. **OWASP Proactive Controls C2: security-library adoption and encapsulation** — https://top10proactive.owasp.org/archive/2018/c2-leverage-security-frameworks-libraries/

   This supplies a practical adoption pattern: assess the source, maintain an inventory, keep components updated, and expose only the behavior the application requires. A narrow application-facing interface can make the dependency's role and replacement points easier to inspect. Encapsulation is not a guarantee that unused library code disappears or that the component is safe. The page identifies itself as the 2018 edition, but I did not establish whether it preceded the 20 April cutoff.

6. **OWASP Dependency-Check** — https://owasp.org/projects/dependency-check

   This is a concrete tool for part of the continuing cost of adoption: identify components and report known disclosed vulnerabilities. It can turn a vague maintenance concern into an explicit scanning and triage task. Its findings depend on supported component identification and vulnerability data; a clean report does not establish correctness, absence of undisclosed flaws, or safe cryptographic use. The current project page was opened, but no dated pre-cutoff release was verified.

7. **npm 5 package-lock.json and integrity verification** — https://blog.npmjs.org/post/161081169345/v500.html

   The release announcement dated 25 May 2017 documents lockfiles, download-integrity checks, and a content-addressed cache. For JavaScript projects, these mechanisms help control what dependency content is installed and reduce accidental variation while keeping the upstream package as a recognizable component. They provide an alternative to copying code simply to obtain predictable builds. A lockfile does not evaluate the selected code or remove the need to review and update it, and the specific implementation is npm-dependent.

For the single-function case, I would first ask whether the behavior is completely understandable and economical to own. For the cryptography case, I would first look for a suitable established API and then budget for correct integration and updates. The middle options above—focused libraries, narrow interfaces, lockfiles, and scanning—make the comparison more useful than a universal rule to either avoid or embrace dependencies.

I would try **BlockTube** first. Its own documentation specifically covers blocking whole YouTube channels, filtering by video title or channel name, and keeping playlists and autoplay usable. It also describes what happens when a blocked video is reached: show a blocked-video page or move on to another video. That makes it the closest documented fit for your concern about an ARTE video starting after a documentary. Sources: [BlockTube documentation](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube) and its [Firefox listing](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/blocktube/).

### Configure it for the channels you encounter

1. Install BlockTube for a browser it supports. The opened official Firefox listing is available, and the repository also describes Chrome support. Your browser and device were not specified, so I have not assumed an exact installation environment.
2. When you encounter an unwanted ARTE upload, use the extension's channel-blocking context-menu action. Repeat for the relevant ARTE channels. For a particular channel, its stable channel ID is preferable to its display name; BlockTube documents that distinction in its [FAQ](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube).
3. If you also want to catch videos whose visible title names ARTE, add `Arte` as a video-title rule. You can likewise use a channel-name rule where appropriate. The [filter documentation](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube/wiki/Filters-Options) says ordinary keywords are case insensitive and each line defines a rule. A title rule may also hide an unrelated video that discusses ARTE, so the channel-specific rule is the more precise starting point.
4. Keep direct-access blocking enabled. If you want playback to continue with another allowed suggestion when blocking occurs, enable the option that advances to the next suggested video. Both controls appear in the [upstream options source](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube/blob/master/src/ui/options.html).

This works by matching channel identities and metadata. It does not establish a guarantee that every third-party reupload of an ARTE production will be recognised when its uploader and title do not identify ARTE. If those reuploads are your problem too, they require additional matching rules or individual video blocks. I checked documentation and source labels; I did not install the extension or run a live autoplay test.

### A useful immediate workaround

If you mainly want the current documentary to end quietly when you fall asleep, turn **YouTube Autoplay off** using the switch in the video player. YouTube's [official instructions](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6327615?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en) explain that Autoplay starts another related video after the current one ends and that the setting can differ between devices.

This is only a workaround for that automatic next-video transition. It does not remove ARTE from search or recommendations, and it stops automatic progression to other related channels as well. I would not infer from this help page that it cancels every existing playlist or Mix continuation.

### Other extensions worth checking

**[Channel Blocker](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/channel-blocker/nfkmalbckemmklibjddenhnofgnfcdfp)** supports blocking individual videos or whole channels and offers regular expressions. Its [upstream repository](https://github.com/Time-Machine-Development/Channel-Blocker-Manifest-v3) confirms that general filtering purpose. However, the official text I opened does not explain whether a blocked channel is prevented from playing when selected as the next video. I would verify that behavior before relying on it for your sleeping scenario. It remains a plausible candidate, not a documented failure.

**[YTBlock](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/ytblock-block-any-content/nedcanggplmbbgmlpcjiafgjcpdimpea)** advertises channel rules, title matching and regular expressions, along with additional metadata filters. Some richer fields, such as tags, categories and descriptions, require a Google API key. Its opened listing likewise does not settle the autoplay question. In addition, that listing is version 6.3.1 updated on November 19, 2026, after your June 9, 2026 question, so it does not by itself establish what was available when you asked.
